UNITED NATIONS 
DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE FRAMEWORK
2002 - 2006
SOUTH AFRICA
30 August 200012
 TABLE OF CONTENTS
I - Rationale
A - Background
B - UNDAF Process and Participation (South Africa)
1. The UN System in South Africa
2. Mandate and Participation
3. Preparation Process
a) Common Country Assessment
b) Harmonized Programme Cycle
c) Scope.
d) UNDAF chronology
C – Key Competencies and Comparative Advantages
II - Goals and Objectives
A – Key Development Challenges
B – Priority Development Goal and UNDAF Objectives 
1. Managing the HIV/AIDS Pandemic
a) Stem the Rate of New Infections
b) Protection, Care and Support for the Infected and the Affected
c) Reduced Overall Impact of HIV/AIDS on Socio-economic 
Development
2. Integrated Sustainable Rural Development
a) Creation of an Enabling Environment
b) Capacity Building for Local Governance to Enhance Service Delivery
c) Enhanced Capacity of Communities to Engage in IRD
3. Regional Integration
a) South Africa’s participation in economic, social and political 
development in the region
III - Cooperation Strategies to Attain UNDAF Objectives
1. HIV/AIDS Prevention Programmes with Focus on Children and Youth
2. Improved Care and Support for People Infected/Affected by AIDS
3. Enabling Environment for those Infected/Affected by HIV/AIDS
4. Integration of HIV Concerns in all Sectors of Society
5. Multi Sectoral Planning, Budgeting, and Implementation in Response
to AIDS
6. Formulation of Operational frameworks for IRD
7. Effective and Efficient Service Delivery by Local Authorities
8. Rural Community Capacity to Engage in IRD
9. Regional Peace, Stability, Democracy and Good Governance
10. Articulation of Regional Poverty Alleviation Policies
11. Enhanced Regional Response to HIV/AIDS
12. Indigenous Knowledge Systems and Exchange of Learning Systems 
13. Disaster Mitigation, Enhanced Disaster Management in SADC Region
IV - Follow-up and Review
V – Programme Resources Framework3
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
The preparation of the United Nations Development Assistance Framework 
(UNDAF) for South Africa, as well as the Common Country Assessment (CCA) on which it 
is based, has moved the United Nations Country Team (UNCT) in South Africa closer toward 
the Secretary General’s vision of a unified UN system at the country level.
Through the CCA/UNDAF process, the UN team in South Africa has assessed the 
major challenges facing its host Government and the opportunities that this provides to shape 
the team’s relations with the country. The system also reviewed its own effectiveness during 
its brief existence in South Africa, and identified weaknesses and strengths. In so doing, the 
Country Team has confirmed the UN’s role in South Africa as a facilitator of international 
practices, norms and standards. Preparing the UNDAF has also highlighted the need for the 
UNCT to engage more forcefully in related advocacy. 
The key development challenges giving shape to the UNDAF, based on priority issues 
targeted by the Government and previewed in the CCA, are summarized in the document. 
Most critical are: 
n The rapidly growing HIV/AIDS epidemic, which has affected up to 4.2 
million South Africans to date. A disproportionately high number of these 
victims are young women. Growing numbers of AIDS orphans and the rapid 
spread of the disease are especially worrisome. 
n The high numbers of poor, particularly in rural areas, and continuing deep
inequalities in the distribution of wealth. Specific programmes have been 
designed to respond to these challenges. These include improved educational 
opportunities, expanded health facilities and more accessible housing. The 
Government is also facilitating the private sector’s capacity to create jobs and 
provides funds for community initiatives.
n A history of alienation within the regional context, with need to further 
improve links to pro-actively resolve issues related to social development, 
HIV/AIDS, crime and drugs, the environment, disaster preparedness, human 
rights, refugees and displaced persons. 
The overall goal of UN assistance in South Africa throughout the period covered by 
the UNDAF will be to achieve a higher state of basic human rights encompassing 
sustained levels of human development to alleviate poverty and inequality and reduce 
the impact and spread of HIV/AIDS. This goal, as articulated by the Government’s Policy 
Coordination and Advisory Services Unit, is based on the priorities of the Government and 
builds on those identified in the CCA. 
More specifically, the Government of South Africa has asked the United Nations
Country Team in South Africa to work toward the following three objectives: 
1. Stemming the HIV/AIDS pandemic by contributing to:
¸ South Africa’s efforts to reduce the rate of new infections;4
¸ The creation of an enabling environment for the protection, care and support for the 
infected and affected, with emphasis on women and children, in particular orphans; 
¸ The reduction of the overall impact of HIV/AIDS on socio-economic development.
2. Improved levels of Integrated Sustainable Rural Development (ISRD) by:
¸ contributing to South Africa’s efforts to create an enabling environment for ISRD to 
eradicate poverty; to create viable sustainable rural economies; and to promote social 
cohesion, thereby enhancing the capacity of rural communities to engage in 
sustainable development and interact productively with urban communities.
3. Intensified Regional Integration by supporting:
¸ South Africa’s participation in economic, social and political development in the 
region, particularly with respect to pressing issues such as crime, drugs, the 
environment, disaster prevention and preparedness, human rights and refugees.
Within this context, the Government of South Africa places great value on the 
capacity of the UN system in South Africa to share its know-how in the development and 
management of data and indicators, and of mechanisms for monitoring and evaluation. 
The UNDAF provides a road map to reach this goal and the objectives that are set out. 
The UNCT agrees that the mechanism established by the UN Theme Group on HIV/AIDS 
serve as a model for addressing the other issues for which the Government has requested 
United Nations assistance. The HIV/AIDS theme group has initiated joint agency assessment 
missions and developed a joint UN work-plan with multi-year goals and objectives, detailing 
individual and collective activities by agencies as well as related resource requirements. Two 
more theme groups are planned along the same lines, to be tasked with developing and 
implementing similar work-plans. 
I - RATIONALE
A - Background
1. Reform of the UN System
As part of the general reform1 of the United Nations System, the Secretary-General 
called in 1997 for greater coordination and resource optimization across the agencies falling 
within the UN operational structures. More particularly, he emphasized greater:
 
1
In his letter of 17 March 1997 to the President of the General Assembly, the UN Secretary General set out his 
ideas for what are called Track-1 Reform Proposals, including those concerning the UN at country level. The 
proposals underlined the need for arrangements to secure greater integration of UN activities, both at UN 
headquarters and at country level. To achieve this objective, the Secretary-General decided to take several 
steps, among which were: strengthening the Resident Coordinator System; preparing a common programme 
framework at the country level; and intensifying the drive to establish common premises and common services 
arrangements. This was in response to the call of Member States who made clear their wish to see greater 
integration of United Nations activities at the country level, nonetheless preserving the special characteristics 
and distinctiveness of the various Funds and Programmes.5
a) Cooperation: both within the UN system (stronger unity of purpose and 
collaboration through a mix of parallel and joint programming among agencies) and 
between the UN system and its Member States governments.
b) Coordination: improved follow-up to UN conferences and support for the 
implementation of conventions and declarations; 
c) Capacity: to effectively and efficiently implement the UN’s development mandate 
(more efficient use of limited resources, based on improved division of labour, 
rationalization of resource allocation and streamlining of procedures); and
d) Clarification: secured role for the UN system in development cooperation with 
recipient Governments taking into account past performance, national needs and 
priorities (improved focus and results orientation, identifying where the UN system 
can have a comparative advantage by using its unique strengths as a development 
partner).
The United Nations Development Assistance Framework aims within this context to 
address the above concerns, with the full endorsement and commitment of all in the UN 
system in South Africa. The UNDAF is a comprehensive, integrated tool to increase the 
impact of UN cooperation on the lives of the most vulnerable and poorest. It is also intended 
to be a strategic document that sets out the motivation for, commitment to, and operational 
planning to realize UN reform. And finally, it is an instrument to achieve cooperation, 
coordination, capacity building, and role clarification for the UN system as an institution. By 
so doing, it will provide a base for greater support for the South African Government’s 
development goals. UNDAF builds on the analysis provided by the Common Country 
Assessment to arrive at coherent strategies for the UN system in South Africa, and will in 
turn serve as the basis for the integrated country programmes to be developed by the 
respective constituents of the UN system in South Africa.
2. Reform and the UN System in South Africa
The collective experience of the UN system in South Africa, during its short history in 
the country2, indicates that the respective agencies need to coordinate their development 
assistance. Less than 2 percent of the South African Government’s development budget is 
derived from international funding sources3. The dispersion of this modest input leads to loss 
of impact. 
UNHCR was first to set up an office in South Africa in 19914 followed by most other 
UN agencies in 1994 and 1995. The FAO and the ODCCP were the last agencies to establish 
 
2
 There was no UN country office presence in South Africa during apartheid so the UN country office is recently 
established. Mutual understandings and synergistic cooperation, and similar characteristics that underlie a solid 
cooperative partnership still need to be nurtured. The UNDAF provides a mechanism to address this need.
3
 For the year 2000, the National Budget is estimated to amount to US$ 36 Billion, total forecast of ODA 
disbursement to US$ 116 Million, or one third of one percent approximately, and expected UN disbursements 
are estimated to amount to US$ 15 Million, 8 percent of ODA and 0.003 percent of the National Budget.
4
“ The Government of the Republic of South Africa and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner 
for Refugees concluded a number of agreements and arrangements, most notably the Memorandum of 
Understanding signed in Geneva on 4th September, 1991.” Source: Basic Agreement Between the Government 
of the Republic of South Africa and the UNHCR Concerning the Presence, Role, Legal Status, Immunities and 
Privileges of the UNHCR and its Personnel in the Republic of South Africa.6
offices in South Africa in 1998. Each agency negotiated its own “basic agreement” with the 
South African Government. Considered within the context of the total development 
assistance provided by all donors and the fact that the UN system in South Africa is lightly 
“resourced5” the motivation for UN agencies to coordinate and cooperate through joint 
programming is strong.
UNDAF, established by General Assembly Resolution 53/192, and confirmed by the 
ACC Statement on implementation of 53/192 and the ACC Guidance Note on the 
implementation of CCA and UNDAF exercises, provides the mechanism and process for 
optimizing the impact of the UN system’s development support. It also facilitates the 
establishment and strengthening of a meaningful relationship within the UN system itself and 
between the system and the South African Government. This point was noted by the UN 
country team in South Africa in a reflective document about lessons learned from the UN’s 
experience for the period 1994 to 1999. The importance of the United Nations agencies in 
South Africa was found to stand out in terms of the knowledge, ideas, experience, and 
technical assistance that they bring to fill specific gaps identified by Government. Given this 
situation, the UN agencies in South Africa, individually and collectively, need to:
q Focus on strategic niches where their work has the most impact;
q Strengthen partnerships among themselves based on close collaboration, pooling of 
resources, joint programming, and effective coordination;
q Forge close collaboration with the South African Government, as well as with 
bilateral donors committed to promoting South African development, civil society, 
and the private sector;
q Sharpen and effectively target their internal and external advocacy work on a few 
critical priority issues in South Africa’s (and Southern Africa’s) development plans; 
and
q Plan their activities carefully and use their limited resources to leverage the larger 
pools of money and personnel available through both the Government’s development 
budget and funds from bilateral donors.6
Coordination of UN assistance programmes is a prerequisite for the UN system to 
provide “value added” to the South African Government. This will ensure that the UN 
resources are optimized and the system’s collective “engagement demands” are lessened. 
Both coordination and cooperation are important if the UN system is to move toward a 
unified response to the South African Government. UNDAF provides a mechanism through 
which to do this. 
The need for coordinated and cooperative “joint programming” is clear, 
notwithstanding reform challenges that stem from individual agency operations. The 
underlying logic is that all UN agencies (funds, programmes, organizations, and 
commissions) share one central preoccupation: the need to reduce poverty and inequality and 
to promote basic human rights. When complemented by the need for overall UN system 
 
5
 South Africa is classified amongst middle-income economies with a per capita GNP in excess of US$ 3000 
per year. As a result, it receives low apportionment in GNP-based UN agency grant allocations, and furthermore 
is not eligible for low interest financial loan assistance. Some bilateral donors do have limited assistance 
programmes targeted on specific issues, mostly linked to the post apartheid transition period. In addition, the 
South African government is reluctant to borrow from the international financial institutions due to the relatively 
high cost in comparison with the bond market.
6
 Source: Annex 2 Review of South Africa/UN Cooperation, 1994-1999, “Lessons Learned from the
Experience of UN Agencies in South Africa” 7
reform, a rights based approach to development assistance emerges as a cross cutting issue 
that binds the UN agency family and transcends individual agency concerns7. This applies 
more generally to the body of UN Conventions and to the continuum of International 
Conferences that South Africa has subscribed to.
B - UNDAF Process and Participation 
1. The UN System in South Africa
Thirteen fully-recognized UN agencies are represented in South Africa (in 
alphabetical order): the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO); International Labour 
Organization (ILO), the Joint United Nations Program on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS); the United 
Nations Office for Drug Control and Crime Prevention (UNDCCP); United Nations 
Development Programme (UNDP), United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA); United 
Nations Education, Science and Culture Organization (UNESCO); United Nations High 
Commission for Human Rights (UNHCHR); United Nations High Commission for Refugees 
(UNHCR); United Nations Information Centre (UNIC); United Nations Children’s Fund 
(UNICEF); United Nations Volunteers (UNV); and the World Health Organization (WHO). 
With the exception of UNDP, UNFPA, UNICEF, and UNIC, all these agencies have 
regional functions and mandates in Southern Africa, extending in some cases to the Horn of 
Africa and the Indian Ocean Islands. UNHCR has its Regional Directorate based in South 
Africa. The majority, with the exception of the ILO and UNDCCP, are located in the UN 
House in Pretoria. The latter plans to join the UN House as soon as space is available there.
The International Organization for Migration (IOM), although not strictly speaking a 
UN Agency, associates itself with most UN activities in South Africa, and also plans to join 
the UN House. The World Bank and International Finance Corporation maintain separate 
regional offices, and the UN Secretariat’s Press Liaison Office, IRIN, is independently 
located in Johannesburg. The UN group meets regularly at the Heads of Agencies level, as 
well as in theme groups. As noted above, the group dealing with HIV/AIDS is particularly 
active.
2. Mandate and Participation
In preparing the UNDAF, the UNCT noted that the UN General Assembly had called 
for the “full and active participation of the funds and programmes, and specialized agencies.” 
It also agreed that drafting the UNDAF is a learning process that will refine the system’s joint 
analysis and programming capacities. 
The challenge for the first UNDAF for South Africa is to move from a situation where 
collaboration and joint programming are the exception, as in the HIV/AIDS theme group, to a 
situation where they are widespread. The Country Team recognizes and accepts that the goal 
of UNDAF is to facilitate the targeting of UN support for the Government’s development 
priorities, so as to increase the impact of the UN cooperation on the lives of the most 
vulnerable and poorest. 
 
7
 In this context, “development assistance” takes on a broad meaning. Through the proclamation of the Right to 
Development and other instruments, the human person has been reaffirmed as the central concern of 
development, with every individual both a contributor to and beneficiary of this right. Source: General 
Assembly resolution A/41/128; General Assembly resolution A/53/1558
3. Preparation Process
a) Common Country Assessment and the UNDAF
Preparation of the Common Country Assessment (CCA), initiated in March 1998, was 
a prerequisite for the UNDAF. The CCA sets out what the country team, in consultation with 
Government representatives, identified as the challenges to transformation confronting the 
Government of South Africa, for the period 1999 to 2004. Six problem areas were identified 
through the CCA: i) economic growth; ii) social cohesion; iii) delivery of basic social 
services; iv) HIV/AIDS; v) environmental concerns; and vi) Southern Africa’s regional 
integration. The CCA was prepared in two stages, under the leadership of an internal 
Secretariat. For the first stage, chaired by the head of UNESCO, the research team included 
the Economic Commission for Africa, which provided useful analysis on the economic trends 
in the country, with most recent data from the Reserve Bank and Statistics South Africa. The 
second stage was chaired by the head of the Policy Coordination and Advisory Services Unit 
in the Office of the Presidency. The Secretariat managed the preparation and completion of 
the CCA, the joint mid-term review of the UN Development Group agencies (UNFPA, 
UNICEF and UNDP) and the agreements on the focus and priorities of the UNDAF, all by 
October 1999. 
Meanwhile, in June 1999, a new Government was elected and assumed office. A brief 
annotated UNDAF outline identifying the proposed priority areas of focus and some key 
lessons of UN experience in South Africa was presented to a meeting of Directors General in 
November 1999. The meeting, chaired by the Head of the Policy Coordination and Advisory 
Services Unit in the Presidency, confirmed the areas of focus for the UNDAF and committed 
to continue its engagement with the process. More specifically, the UN system was asked to 
focus its assistance on three of the new leadership’s six priority areas: i) Integrated 
Sustainable Rural Development; ii) HIV/AIDS; and iii) Regional Integration. In the final 
preparation phase, during the first half of the year 2000, the Government has been kept 
closely informed and recently identified the new Chief Director for Social Development in 
the Presidency as the new UNDAF focal point. Two retreats took place, a one-day retreat in 
March to refine the concepts and a three day retreat early in July to agree on objectives and 
outputs.
In reviewing the linkages between the CCA and the three themes identified by the 
Government, the UN Country Team confirmed the convergence of priorities. Specifically, 
“Managing the Challenge of HIV/AIDS” corresponds directly with the Government’s focus 
on the same issue. The CCA priority of “Enhancing Southern African Regional Integration” 
corresponds directly with the Government’s interest in regional integration. Finally, the CCA 
priority of “Improved Delivery of Basic Social Services,” while not focusing exclusively on 
rural areas, highlighted the challenges faced by local governance structures in their efforts to 
enhance integrated development. The emphasis on integrated governance mechanisms at the 
local level is an important development and presents an opportunity for enhanced urban-rural 
complementarity through shared learning from previous decentralized governance 
experiences. 
b) Harmonized Programme Cycle9
The UNDAF is intended to have the same duration as the harmonized programme 
cycles of the UNDG agencies in South Africa. The ongoing cycles of UNDP, UNFPA, and 
UNICEF are fully synchronized 1997 to 2001, and again from 2002 to 2006. (note: WFP and 
IFAD, which are also part of UNDG, do not have programmes in the country). Other 
agencies have shorter cycles, which fit in well within this context. The 1999 Mid-Term 
Review of the operating UNDG agencies (UNICEF, UNFPA and UNDP) provides a practical 
example of the harmonization of country programmes. The MTR focused on five critical 
themes - including operational decision making - which were important to all three 
programmes rather than to each participating agency. This harmonization of procedures will 
be pursued and mainstreamed in an inclusive manner so as to enlarge the common pool of 
activities. Agency Headquarters are also working on the harmonization of the various policies 
and procedures at their level.
c) Scope
In accordance with Government’s advice, the Country Team has built the UNDAF on 
the three major objectives identified and communicated by the Government’s DirectorsGeneral in the above mentioned meeting in late 1999: HIV/AIDS, Integrated Sustainable 
Rural Development (ISRD), and Regional Integration (RI). However, the evolving nature of 
development goals in a country in transition coupled with the interrelated nature of ongoing 
government priorities justifies an annual review mechanism led by government, to ensure that 
the scope of the UNDAF remains true to the needs of the day. The UN team fully subscribes 
to the Government’s request that it should target the three provinces identified as most 
needing of assistance: KwaZulu Natal, Northern Province, and Eastern Cape. However, the 
team also recognizes the existence of pockets of poverty in all six of the remaining provinces, 
which may justify selective exceptions to the three concentration provinces.
HIV/AIDS will serve as the first objective because of the tremendous challenge it 
represents for the future of South Africa and the sub-region, as well as for other parts of the 
continent. Rates of prevalence are in the double digits, projected deaths in the millions, and 
the implications on every aspect of social and economic life are shattering. The UN system 
has a great comparative advantage in this respect because each agency has given considerable 
thought and accumulated valuable experience with respect to the implications that HIV/AIDS 
has on its area of competence. This is then complemented by the presence of the UNAIDS 
Inter-Country Team which is active in the country.
Integrated Sustainable Rural Development (ISRD) is the second issue selected for 
integrated programming. Local governments and communities face major challenges in 
dealing with decentralization and participatory governance, especially in rural areas where 
local government structures and systems are still evolving. Given this need, the country team 
agrees that this is also an area in which the UN experience and know how is cross cutting and 
able to provide valuable insights and support to the Government’s efforts. Complementarity 
with UN know-how and efforts in the area of urban decentralized decision making will also 
be an asset.
Regional Integration (RI) is an important issue for the South African Government, 
both within and outside its borders. South Africa needs constructive interaction in the region. 
The Government has been able to establish itself in the sub-region as a partner on significant 
political, social, economic and trade issues. It has also played a key role in attempting to 
mediate conflicts and other forms of civil strife, and provided some economic development 10
support for countries in crisis. Regional integration opens up opportunities for UN agencies to 
avail the Government of their regional and sub-regional networking capacities and knowhow, the more so because the majority of UN agencies in South Africa already have a 
regional mandate, and the UNDAF provides an opportunity to draw these capacities together 
in cohesion. 
d) UNDAF Chronology
The UNDAF time frame relates to the period 2002 - 2006. The UNDG agencies have 
synchronized their programmes to this period. However, the country team has agreed that for 
operational purposes the UNDAF will become effective on signature. Other agencies have 
one or two-year programming periods which can at least partially be made to fit within the 
above time frame. Country programmes being elaborated from now on will use the UNDAF 
as their frame of reference.
C - Key Competencies and Comparative Advantages
At a retreat in May 1998, the UN Country Team identified the UN’s key comparative 
advantages in South Africa, based on the diversity and multidisciplinary nature of all 
agencies present, including the regional offices, as: 
q Presentation and adherence to international standards and practices, including 
declarations, conventions, and the UN conference continuum;
q Advocacy for people centered and rights based development policies and strategies; 
q Access to universal and regional databanks;
q Support to South Africa’s regional and global re-integration; 
q Universality and impartiality; and
q Capacity to play a facilitating role between external and internal parties.
II - GOALS AND OBJECTIVES
A - Key development challenges
The main issues confronting South Africa today, identified by the CCA, and 
confirmed by the new Government’s policies, are HIV/AIDS, delivery of basic services, 
including education, health services, housing and water, job creation, and crime prevention. 
They impact differently on the three objectives selected for the UN system in South Africa:
HIV/AIDS - The rapidly growing HIV/AIDS epidemic, (with HIV prevalence rates 
estimated to be between 10 and 20 percent of the adult population) has forced South Africa to 
place this challenge at the very top of its list of priorities. The Government of South Africa 
recognizes that investing in HIV/AIDS is no longer one among several options, it is the 
precondition for investment in other sectors. Currently there are up to 4.2 million South 
Africans living with HIV. The National Adolescent Sexual Health Initiative estimates that 
more than 50 percent of South Africans under 20 years of age today (July 2000) will die from 
AIDS-related diseases before they are 35. By the year 2005, there may be six million South 
Africans infected with HIV and almost one million children under the age of 15 whose 
mothers will have died of AIDS. Poverty, high unemployment and marginalization of men 
increase the spread. In rural communities women are often trapped in abusive relationships 
due to economical and cultural dependence on their partners for food, shelter and money. 11
This dependency results in a higher level of rape and other forms of violence against women 
which in turn also puts the women living in an abuse relationship in greater danger of 
contracting HIV/AIDS. Drug and alcohol abuse also contribute to the spread, by fostering 
violent and abusive relationships. Under the effect of both drugs and alcohol, people tend to 
engage in irresponsible sexual behavior, which again contributes to the spread of HIV/AIDS.
The Partnership Against AIDS campaign, which is guided by an Inter-Ministerial 
committee chaired by the Deputy President, was launched in 1998. A National Council on 
HIV and AIDS, launched early in 2000, oversees the policies and programmes that are 
developed across sectors with a broad range of partners in business and civil society. These 
high-level initiatives are complemented by numerous other campaigns and programmes 
driven from within government and civil society organizations, in particular those of People 
Living with HIV and AIDS. The recent International conference on HIV/AIDS held in South 
Africa served as an important advocacy opportunity to focus attention on the epidemic. The 
challenge of HIV and AIDS has been identified as the major programme focus area for UN 
support to South Africa, especially because it is so intricately linked to all other national 
development priorities. All organizations are striving to place strong emphasis on integrating 
HIV and AIDS into existing and planned programmes as a matter of urgency in the context of 
a joint workplan of the UN Theme Group on HIV and AIDS. 
Addressing Rural Poverty – Estimates of the incidence and depth of poverty in 
South Africa vary. Based on consumption expenditure levels consistent with the minimum 
level of food intake (calorific consumption), which usually defines the "absolute poverty" 
level, it is estimated that about 40 percent of the South African population may be considered 
poor. Poverty is not confined to any one race group, but is heavily concentrated among black 
people: up to 61 percent of Africans and 38 percent of Coloureds are poor, compared with 5 
percent of Indians and 1 percent of Whites. Most of the poor live in rural areas: while roughly 
50 percent of the population of South Africa is rural, the rural areas contain 72 percent of 
those members of the total population who are poor.8
The Government of South Africa has actively participated in the implementation of 
the World Summit for Social Development and holds the Chair of the UN Commission for 
Social Development. The government has demonstrated its commitment to eradicating 
poverty by increasing levels of expenditure on social development and establishing a Poverty 
Relief Fund that facilitates inter-departmental and departmental support to anti-poverty 
initiatives in collaboration with community organizations and other organs of civil society. 
This in addition to the ongoing programmes of line departments designed to address poverty 
and inequality within the framework of the Reconstruction and Development Program. Urban 
poverty is being addressed through several large scale projects supported by government and 
various donors, including an upcoming urban municipality support programme with the 
World Bank, and it is in this context that the government has identified Integrated Sustainable 
Rural Development as a priority for UN support during the current governing period.
Regional Integration - Declining gold prices, privatization of parastatals, the “right 
sizing” (reduction) of the public sector and the contentious issues of employment quality in 
progressive labour law legislation have slowed an effective increase in jobs creation. 
Unemployment remains very high, ranging between 23 and 38 percent depending on the 
definition used, and has been increasing recently, endangering social and labour market 
 
8
 South Africa Common Country Assessment, 1999 12
stability. In the context of migration, while economic disparities between the Southern 
African countries create a climate of xenophobia in the wealthier countries, the SADC Treaty 
calls for the development of policies aimed at the free movement of people. In order to 
address these problems properly, it is essential for the government to embark on and 
contribute to full adherence to regional and international conventions. High levels of crime, 
including drug-related crime, have a negative impact on the South African society, affecting 
not only the economy and social environment but posing a serious threat to the country’s new 
democracy. With 35 percent of South Africans being victimized by any crime during the 
course of a year, the level of crime is severely testing the Government’s capacity to provide 
its citizens with a secure environment. This is especially true for part of the population, with 
Africans being 20 times more at risk from homicide than whites, and 95 percent of all rapes 
being committed on African women (1995 data). The above issues are also part of the debate 
around regional integration. Transnational crime and corruption cannot be fought by one 
country in isolation. Regional and international cooperation is crucial in this regard. 
Similarly, issues relating to the environment, to disaster prevention and preparedness, to 
human rights and refugees, are better addressed from a regional perspective.
South Africa has been playing a major role in the rejuvenation of SADC, and many 
successes have been scored in regional cooperation. However, a number of intractable 
differences still persist, for which further dialogue will be required. The continuum of UN 
Conferences, the UN system’s ready access to data and information, the UN Conventions, 
can provide valuable references in this context.
B - Priority Development Goal and UNDAF Objectives
The root causes of the challenges confronting South Africa today can be seen from the 
perspective of the capacity to ensure rights based sustainable livelihoods to the whole 
population. Having considered its collective comparative advantages, the Country Team has 
concluded that Stemming HIV/AIDS, Integrated Sustainable Rural Development, and
Regional Integration are the objectives to which the system can aim to provide leverage 
during the next programming period, and by which each of the UN agencies will be guided in 
its country programming. In a more cross cutting way, support for the development and 
management of development indicators and mechanisms for monitoring and evaluation is 
also a critical objective for urgent capacity building.
These three objectives are integrated through the overarching goal which is to achieve 
a higher state of basic human rights encompassing sustained levels of human 
development to alleviate poverty and inequality and reduce the impact and spread of 
HIV/AIDS. This goal is consistent with the “Declaration on the Right to Development” 
which affirms the human being as the “central subject of development” and “the active 
participant and beneficiary of the right to development”. Through this overarching goal, the 
UN agencies will orient their country programmes to address development concerns within 
the three inter-related objectives. The Development Assistance Framework for the UN system

More specifically, the UN in South Africa aims to contribute to the three objectives 
stated above by producing the following outcomes:
1. Managing the HIV/AIDS Pandemic
The challenge of managing the HIV/AIDS pandemic, and in particular its 
development implications for South Africa, warrants a primary focus from all UN agencies in 
South Africa. The UN Country Team agrees that the UN is particularly well placed to 
contribute in three areas: prevention, care and support, and mitigation. Each of these areas is 
articulated in the form of a sub-objective to which the UN will contribute, based on specific 
programming outcomes. The sub-objectives are: 
a) Stemming the Rate of New Infections
The UN team in South Africa recognizes that the challenge of HIV/AIDS intersects 
with different levels of government, across all sectors, and with society at large. For example, 
the vulnerability of women, children and youth warrant specific attention from the UN 
Country Team. The principle of “Greater Involvement of People Living with AIDS” (GIPA) 
is vital in the attempts to prevent, provide care and support and mitigate HIV/AIDS because it 
acknowledges the critical role that people living with the disease can play in the national 
response. 
The CCA highlights the direct link between gender inequities in the country, and the 
HIV/AIDS epidemic. Its implications for children (e.g. mother to child transmission) and 
youth are clear. In recognition of the link between HIV/AIDS and sexual violence against 
women, the UNDAF includes a cooperation strategy specifically targeting that tragic problem 
of gender inequality. This results in the UNDAF’s first programming outcome, which is
Support to the expansion and effectiveness of prevention programmes with special focus 
on children, youth and other vulnerable groups.
b) Creation of an Enabling Environment for the Protection, Care, and Support of 
Those Infected and Affected by HIV/AIDS
A continuing high incidence rate of HIV/AIDS threatens to reverse gains in human 
development and raises issues of human rights such as dignity, equality, and access to basic 
services (e.g., health care). Such matters are at the core of the need to create an enabling 
environment to protect, care for and support members of society infected or affected by 
HIV/AIDS, in particular children who are the most vulnerable.14
In partnership with local governance structures, civil society and people living with 
HIV/AIDS, the UN system support will emphasize care and support for infected and affected 
children. Orphans will receive special attention. Assistance will also target young women and 
HIV positive mothers. The CCA notes that “HIV prevalence among women attending 
antenatal clinics has increased twenty-fold over the past eight years to over 22.8% by the end 
of 1998. The rate of increase among teenagers (15 – 19) was highest in 1998 (65.4% from 
1997 to 1998) in comparison with percentage increase rates of 32.5% and 47.8% among 
women in their twenties, 20-24 and 25-29 years old respectively9”
This increase in the incidence of HIV/AIDS among young women of child bearing
age has a direct impact on children through mother-to-child transmission (infection) or family 
disruption when women either die or are unable to provide for their children (affected). 
Given the broad social, economic, political, and cultural impact of HIV/AIDS, the team aims 
to emphasize care and support to children. The estimate of one million orphans by the year 
2005 gives an idea of the degree to which the usual hosting systems, grandparents or small 
NGOs, are going to be over extended, and the need for fresh solutions. The United Nations 
agencies must direct specific capacity-building support to the caregivers of children infected 
and affected by HIV/AIDS. At the community level, these caregivers are usually women 
(often grandmothers), who require access to information, income, healthcare, and social 
support systems. Within this context, the second programming outcome that the UN system 
in South Africa aims to achieve through help to government, NGOs, key partners and 
communities, is Improved care and support for people infected and affected, with special 
emphasis on children, particularly orphans, and their support systems.
The care and support of people infected and affected by HIV/AIDS requires a 
supportive environment within which people can be encouraged to test voluntarily and openly 
declare their status without fear of loss of dignity, equality, or freedom – fundamental human 
rights. Since youth are a high-risk group, places of learning become central points for 
reducing stigma and discrimination. The workplace is another environment wherein stigma 
and discrimination may prevail. Therefore, it must be a concentration point for the building of 
trust and respect so that those infected and affected can be supported and cared for. In terms 
of the large percentage of unemployed individuals outside schools, the community is left as a 
critical place of engagement. For these reasons, the UNDAF’s third programming outcome is
to provide an effective contribution to The establishment of an enabling environment in 
communities, learning institutions and in the workplace, including the public service, 
which protects human rights and reduces stigma and discrimination for those infected 
and affected by HIV/AIDS.
c) Reduce the overall impact of HIV/AIDS on socio-economic development
Reversal of the current trend of HIV infections in the country requires multi-sectoral 
intervention at all levels, especially in communities. It requires a coordinated and integrated 
partnership among community-based organizations, non-governmental organizations, local 
government, trade unions, other development role players, and the private sector. 
Consistent with the government’s HIV/AIDS/STD Strategic Plan for South Africa 
2000-2005, the national response is not the sole responsibility of the health sector. The plan is 
 
9
 vide CCA15
a “statement for the country as a whole, both within and outside government. It is recognized 
that no single sector, ministry, department or organization is by itself responsible for 
addressing the HIV epidemic.”10 Any attempts to reduce the socio-economic impact of 
HIV/AIDS will require more robust inter-sectoral responses to the epidemic as a critical 
strategy for integrating HIV concerns in all sectors of society. The fourth outcome that the 
UNDAF proposes to achieve is therefore the Integration of HIV concerns in all sectors of 
society.
The UN Country Team recognizes the need for greater coordination and integration of 
efforts through multi-sectoral planning, budgeting and implementation and has, therefore, 
agreed that the UN system should facilitate a multi-sectoral approach. It is envisaged that the 
Government will continue to develop a comprehensive HIV/AIDS budget identifying the role 
of all sectors. The UN system will support these efforts with particular emphasis at the 
district council level by building on the Integrated Development Planning mechanism. The 
UN will also try to ensure adequate coverage of care and support, prevention and integration 
strategies. The fifth programming outcome, which the UNDAF aims to achieve in this 
context, is therefore the Successful advocacy of multi-sectoral planning, budgeting and 
implementation in response to the HIV/AIDS epidemic.
2. Integrated Sustainable Rural Development (ISRD)
ISRD has traditionally been seen as a top down approach, i.e., development policy 
formulated at national level trickling down to communities and municipalities. Contemporary 
thinking reverses this model and places the individual at the center. The ideological basis for 
this is captured in the UN’s Declaration on the Right to Development which is consistent 
with South Africa’s current Municipal Systems Bill11 and the Draft Green Paper on 
Development and Planning12. 
ISRD in South Africa is about correcting the socio-economic and political inequities 
of the past, which have resulted in an uneven distribution of basic services, ownership of 
land, participation in public policy formulation, implementation and evaluation; and income 
generation opportunities. The result of such inequities has been a situation of extreme poverty 
for most historically disadvantaged rural communities. These rural communities are largely 
dependent on the remittances generated in urban areas. There are few, if any, activities aimed 
at production or processing which directly benefit these areas. As a result of past agricultural, 
industrial and, perhaps most important of all, land alienation policies, no economic 
investment has taken place in the ex-homeland areas.
 
10 Draft Document – HIV/AIDS/STD Strategic Plan for South Africa 2000-2005 May 2000
11 Essentially, the Municipal Systems Bill promotes a bottom up approach to community development by 
requiring local level government (municipalities) to develop and implement processes and mechanisms for 
public participation regarding municipality development. The Bill asserts its’ purpose to be, amongst others, “to 
provide for the core principles, mechanisms and processes that are necessary to enable municipalities to move 
progressively towards the social and economic upliftment of communities, and ensure universal access to 
essential services that are affordable to all; to define the legal nature of municipality as including residents and 
communities within the municipal area, working in partnership with the municipality’s political and 
administrative structures; to provide for public participation”
12 The Draft Green Paper on Development and Planning sets out the framework for appropriate policies and 
laws regarding the way in which planning and development should be carried out so as to reverse the divisive 
and discriminatory legacy of apartheid. Like the Municipal Systems Bill, this Green Paper emphasizes the need 
for meaningful public consultation and engagement.16
 In many cases, human capital migration has resulted in these areas being populated 
by the elderly, the sickly and the young. The result: social fragmentation. The reduction and 
eradication of poverty through the creation of viable/sustainable rural economies is, therefore, 
the primary focus of ISRD. Sustainability can only be achieved when rural communities have 
the capacity to engage in development. But in South Africa, communities are not yet 
empowered to tackle their own development problems. And local government is not yet 
adequately equipped and skilled to fully involve families and communities in decisions that 
affect their own situation and reality. Local government also has limited experience working 
together in an integrated and cross-sectoral manner. In a community, most problems are 
interrelated. In Government and in development agencies, most problems are tackled in an 
isolated, sectoral manner and then imposed in a vertical, top-down process. This pattern must 
be broken. Communities must be enabled to fully participate in the assessment and analysis 
of their situations, prioritization of their problems and programming of relevant interventions. 
Capacities must be developed for local government officials and community leaders to 
facilitate and manage such processes. 
In his address at the opening of Parliament in June 1999, the President announced that 
his Administration was now ready to implement an integrated rural development strategy. 
This statement must be viewed within the context of the theme of the speech – building on 
the foundations of the first five years –, which implied that the Government was committed to 
developing and implementing a rural development strategy. Government recognizes that 
although significant human development has occurred in rural areas since 1994, much more 
needs to be done. In discussions and documents drafted to explore the strategy for ISRD, it is 
acknowledged that the traditional classification of “rural” in South Africa needs to be 
reviewed to include small towns and semi-urban areas. For example, in the formerly white 
areas there was a concerted effort to ensure that rural towns developed based on agricultural 
or mining activity. In contrast, in the black areas the policy was to create settlements, which 
served as a living abode for labor. There were no income earning opportunities for the 
families of urban employment seekers or retired black workers. The result is that the postApartheid Government inherited clearly defined areas that are devoid of social and economic 
infrastructure. Pockets of poverty and social deprivation dependent on “nearby” agriculture or 
mining developments, which in some cases no longer exist, characterize these areas.
 
a) Creation of an Enabling Environment for Integrated Sustainable Rural 
Development to Eradicate Poverty; 
The national capacities and capabilities regarding ISRD need to be strengthened for a 
variety of reasons:13
ß Rural issues are not reflected as a critical priority in the programmes of departments 
and there are no clear strategies and interventions that speak to the particular 
development challenges faced by rural communities;
ß There is a lack of integration at the national and provincial departmental levels with 
respect to service delivery and interventions. Departments work in isolation and 
reflect no joint prioritization, programming and interventions that will allow for more 
comprehensive servicing, the reduction of duplication and saving of costs;
 
13 Department of Welfare, Second Draft, Integrated Rural Development Framework, Operational Strategy 
Framework, February 2000, 17
ß There is no viable fast tracking delivery approach and little related capacity. The 
urgent need for rural intervention is subject to the normal pace of government, often 
resulting in rural communities not receiving any benefits at all;
ß Local government is not factored into strategy development and implementation 
design at the national and provincial levels. However, local government is tasked with 
the responsibility to develop integrated development plans and localized service 
delivery and maintenance; and 
ß There is no clear definition of integrated rural development and the implications for 
governance at all levels.
Within this context, the sixth programming outcome, which the UNDAF aims to 
achieve, is the Provision of significant and effective support in the formulation of the 
operational frameworks for ISRD strategy at national, provincial and local levels.
. b) CapacityBuilding for Local Governance to Enhance Service Delivery
The Municipal Systems Bill and the Green Paper on Development Planning both 
emphasize public participation as a critical component for integrated development planning. 
The challenge is therefore to assist local structures within Government and civil society to 
enable decentralized decision making within a “governance” framework. Mechanisms for 
social mobilization, economic resource mobilization, public participation, information 
collection and provision, communication, planning and human resource developments are 
critical capacity building requirements for effective governance.
 Moreover, explicit linkages are needed between decentralized governance and 
service delivery through information systems that monitor, evaluate and report on the quality 
of governance and service delivery. Some of the specific “capacities” required for 
decentralized governance through local government are:
ß To facilitate rural households and groups to set priorities, plan, organize, mobilize and 
lead toward the nexus of demand driven rural development. This capacity exists in 
many NGOs and CBOs and other national institutions but needs to be mobilized by 
local government;
ß Capacity to attract and mobilize resources for economic development and social 
services from government departments and the private sector;
ß Capacity to manage their own systems and contractual transactions with service 
providers, to implement and deliver, monitor and evaluate, strong leadership, and 
change management; and
ß Improved data collection for, inter alia, planning for infrastructure development and 
improved services.
The seventh outcome, which the UN system in South Africa therefore undertakes to
deliver as part of the UNDAF is: Capacity building for decentralized governance to 
ensure effective and efficient service delivery
c) Promotion of Social Cohesion through Support to the Enhancement of the Capacity 
of Rural communities to engage in Sustainable Development18
Enhanced capacity for rural communities to engage in sustainable development 
necessarily includes the capacity to articulate effective demand for services at household and 
group level. To this effect, capacity needs to be built in the following areas:
ß Local capacity of rural inhabitants to set priorities for their own communities 
(particularly in response to HIV/AIDS);
ß Capacity of groups to organize themselves, through effective and democratic bodies;
ß Capacity to mobilize and attract resources, including under-utilized government 
development funds;
ß Strong leadership capacity;
ß Capacity for conflict management; and
ß Capacity to absorb external intervention or support.
The eighth outcome, which the UNDAF aims to achieve, is the Enhanced capacity 
for rural communities to engage in the process of sustainable development.
3. Regional Integration
Enhancing Southern African regional integration was highlighted in the CCA as one 
of the six challenges facing South Africa. The CCA notes that regional integration includes 
the need to strengthen regional infrastructure (SADC institutions); to promote cooperation 
with agriculture and food production; to advocate for trade and debt reduction; to regulate 
migration and combat xenophobia; and to coordinate regional responses to HIV/AIDS.14
 Within the context of the UNDAF, regional integration is about support to South 
Africa’s pro-active role within SADC and contributions to regional human development. 
South Africa’s need for assistance from the UN to integrate in the region is based on the 
Apartheid regime’s historical relationship with neighboring countries, which was a source of 
on-going tension deleterious to the regional economy. South Africa recognizes that its 
achievement of sustainable human development and transformation requires the same for the 
Southern African region as a whole. The Government therefore aims to demonstrate its role 
as a SADC member country committed to increase economic cooperation, coordination, and 
integration. Within this context, UNDAF proposes to contribute to the creation of an enabling 
environment for economic, social and political development in the region.
Economic integration, together with regional solidarity and peace, are the most 
important components of effective regional integration15. The Department of Foreign Affairs 
document entitled “Framework for Cooperation with the Countries in the South African 
Region” spells out South Africa’s regional foreign policy objectives. The main emphasis is 
directed towards the maximization of each country’s potential in the region for16:
ß Democratization;
ß Peace and Security (human rights and democracy);
ß Consensus within the region (unity of vision amongst stakeholders e.g., NGOs, CBOs, 
Governments, parastatals, development agencies, private sector, and unions);
 
14 CCA, Annex 4, CCA Conclusions, Challenges for the Governing Period 1999-2004 
15 Letter from the Department of Foreign Affairs to the Resident Coordinator of 8 June 2000
16 Department of Foreign Affairs, Framework for Cooperation with the Countries in the Southern African 
Region, August 199619
ß Cooperation in developing an effective growth and development strategy based on 
equity, mutual benefits and environmental sustainability (promotion of economic 
growth, food security and development); and
ß Linkage of reconstruction and development in the region.
South Africa’s relations with its neighboring states involve technical cooperation, 
trade links, crime prevention, environmental issues, water and sanitation, refugees, tourism, 
migration, cooperation in respect of transport and communications infrastructure, disaster 
mitigation, and power generation. In regard to South Africa’s re-integration within SADC, 
the UN can play an important role in facilitating the transfer of Southern African experiences, 
ideas, and expertise to the benefit of the region. 
The above informs the ninth programming outcome of the UNDAF, Support to 
South Africa’s Contribution towards Regional Peace, Stability, Democracy and Good 
Governance.
Regional integration cannot be based solely on state to state cooperation. It also 
involves the private sector, civil society, the informal sector, and the media, the involvement 
of who forms the basis of good governance. Clearly, regional integration is itself an 
integrated and coordinated activity e.g., political instability in one country will have adverse 
economic consequences for other countries on the continent through reductions in 
investments and/or tourism. Policies that are oriented towards poverty reduction in the region 
are necessary. Such policies could sustain the move away from notions of macroeconomic 
development that accentuate individual states’ economic growth to the detriment of 
surrounding states. They can focus on the challenge of building and sustaining individual 
livelihoods at the household and community levels. As a result of this logic, the tenth 
programming outcome, towards the achievement of which the UNDAF aims to contribute, is 
the Enhanced Capacity for Articulating Relevant Economic Policies for Poverty 
Alleviation in the Region.
Labour migration and its regulation is a critical aspect in the HIV/AIDS management 
challenge. Inter-state responses which target specific sectors - for example, the mining sector 
and migrant workers - present options for developing viable management responses to 
HIV/AIDS, particularly the perception in neighbouring countries that the disease and related 
problems come from South Africa. Partnerships between and among government agencies 
and civil society are necessary since, through migration, the HIV/AIDS pandemic does not 
respect state borders. The eleventh programming outcome of the UNDAF is therefore the 
Provision of Effective and Efficient Support to Enhanced Regional Responses to 
HIV/AIDS Interventions and Partnerships.
The notion of an “African Renaissance” underpins South Africa’s focus on supporting 
the creation and exchange of knowledge systems and processes within the region. A 
prerequisite for knowledge exchange is the existence of learning systems that tap into, and 
document, indigenous norms, mores, healing practices, decision making and governance 
structures, culture and ideology, and education systems in individual Southern African states 
and/or the region collectively. South Africa’s challenge is to support the African Renaissance 
through the creation and exchange of learning and knowledge systems, and to ensure that 
disadvantaged groups, including women, are recognized in the process. This justifies the 
twelfth UNDAF outcome, which is to encourage Policies Aimed at the Promotion of 20
Indigenous Knowledge Systems and Exchange of Learning Systems and Experience in 
the Region.
Southern Africa has suffered more than its share of natural and other disasters. South 
Africa has a unique capacity to assist its neighbors when disasters do occur, and the region 
provides scope for enhanced interaction from a disaster prevention and mitigation 
perspective. Hence, the thirteenth and final outcome to the achievement of which the 
UNDAF aims to contribute is to provide effective support to South Africa’s Efforts towards 
Mitigation of Disasters and Disaster Management in the Region.
III - COOPERATION STRATEGIES
This section provides a summary of how the UN system in South Africa plans to 
achieve the UNDAF objectives. These strategies were agreed upon over the course of a threeday workshop, which took place early in July 2000 and represents the UN consensus. Some 
of the strategies detailed below call for specific joint projects, while others will be carried out 
through convergent advocacy or policy dialogue. Some require joint funding; others will be a 
matter of concerted facilitation of access to existing data and research. The commonality is in 
the interactive working of the UN system to deliver assistance effectively, as much as in joint 
programming or shared funding endeavors.
HIV/AIDS
Outcome 1: To Support the Expansion and Effectiveness of Prevention Programmes 
with Special Focus on Children, Youth and other Vulnerable Groups
The cooperation strategies relating to this outcome will be to:
• Support the design and implementation of programmes addressing violence against 
women and gender inequality;
• Advocate for, and support, the establishment of AIDS education and services in 
learning institutions, the workplace and the community;
• Support national efforts to prevent mother-to-child transmission;
• Support communication strategies for specific audiences, especially youth and men;
• Promote user friendly reproductive health services for all;
• Advocate universal availability of affordable drugs, especially to pregnant, HIV 
positive mothers and to rape victims, inter alia, through negotiations with relevant 
pharmaceutical companies;
• Support interventions to mitigate factors that enhance and accelerate opportunistic 
diseases associated with HIV/AIDS, i.e. poverty reduction, and nutrition;
• Work with national, provincial and local government in identified provinces to 
improve service delivery through policy development, process management, 
monitoring and evaluation;
• Support the improvement and expansion of existing surveillance instruments to 
identify neglected vulnerable groups;
• Encourage collaborative partnerships for promoting an integrative approach in 
response to HIV/AIDS;
• Share international experience and best practice with local partners.21

Efforts to Achieve Improved Care and Support for People Infected and Affected with 
HIV/AIDS, with Special Emphasis on Children, particularly Orphans, and their 
Support Systems
The cooperation strategies relating to this outcome will be to:
• Support the design and development of community based care programmes that focus 
on children and families affected by HIV/AIDS, particularly orphans;
• Contribute to the development of partnerships with decentralized structures (local 
government and civil society) including through capacity building and policy 
dialogue;
• Advocate for adequate communication mechanisms through mutual learning, study 
tours, sharing of best practice, cultural specific drama to create safe spaces that are

Communities, Learning Institutions and in the Workplace which protects Human 
Rights and reduces Stigma and Discrimination for those Infected and Affected by 
HIV/AIDS

protection of rights;

• Encourage the building of trust, respect and partnerships between men and women, 
youth and older people, local government and civil society, infected and non infected

• Promote supportive community norms and values;

workplace.

The cooperation strategies relating to this outcome will be to:
• Identify key entry points through existing programmes and partnerships of the UN 
system;
• Build partnerships with government, business, labour movements, NGOs, and civil 
society to enhance the multi-sectoral response;
• Continue to advocate for multi-sectoral approaches and promote policy dialogue 
through sharing of information and international best practices;22
• Support the application of GIPA in all sectors of the society.
Outcome 5: Successful Advocacy of Multi-Sectoral Planning, Budgeting and 
Implementation in response to HIV/AIDS
The cooperation strategies relating to this outcome will be to:
• Involve all stakeholders in formulating and implementing programmes to ensure a

and reviews of existing programmes to identify critical gaps and duplication as 
required to develop a coherent multi-sectoral response;

living with HIV/AIDS.
Outcome 12: Promote Indigenous Knowledge Systems and Exchange of Learning
Systems and Experiences in the Region
The cooperation strategies relating to this outcome will be to: 
• Advocate for support to, and implementation of, pertinent UN resolutions and 
conventions relating to international cooperation;
• Encourage the application of international norms pertaining to intellectual property so 
as to cover natural products and traditional knowledge in the region;25
• Facilitate intra-regional research and the creation of databanks by universities and 
research institutions linked to existing regional networks;
• Support debates, awareness campaigns and other activities related to cultural 
identities and indigenous knowledge systems within the African Renaissance 
network;
• Ensure the inclusion of women and gender issues in the conceptualization and 
implementation of the African Renaissance
• Advocate and promote harmonization of various certification systems in the region;
• Support efforts for popular mobilization and volunteer work for grassroots 
development and solidarity in the region including social capital creation through 
rotating cultural festivals, exchanges of students and other cultural exchanges;
• Promote initiatives such as the regional peace parks concept and trans-frontier 
conservation areas.
Outcome 13: Mitigate the Impact of Disasters and Enhance Disaster Management in 
the Region
The cooperation strategies relating to this outcome will be to:
• Facilitate networking through existing UN offices in the region of national, regional 
and local authorities dealing with potential disaster areas, such as water management; 
nutrition; public health; and oil spills to promote prevention and mitigation of future 
trans-border disasters in collaboration with existing UN disaster mandated bodies;
• Ensure sharing of successful disaster prevention experiences and lessons learned 
throughout the region;
• Network with UN offices in the region to survey existing disaster management teams 
and initiate and facilitate interaction amongst them in close collaboration with 
existing global disaster management bodies;
• Advocate and support the enhancement of provision within existing government 
structures for prevention and mitigation of disasters that might have trans-border 
implications, including preventive measures.
IV - FOLLOW-UP & REVIEW
In response to the UNDAF and the workplans of the proposed theme groups, the UN 
Country Team is committed to continuing with the harmonized cycles of the UNDG 
agencies. In that context, the UNCT has agreed to an UNDAF covering the period 2002 -
2006, with the eighteen months preceding inception also covered by the process. All agencies 
will develop individual country programmes within the agreed upon frameworks. They will 
focus primarily on the three provinces identified by the government as the most vulnerable: 
Kwa-Zulu Natal, Northern Province and the Eastern Cape, recognizing that pockets of deep 
poverty and vulnerability exist in all other provinces, which may warrant support on an 
exceptional basis. 
The UNCT undertakes to build on the experience of the HIV/AIDS Theme Group and 
to develop theme groups along the same lines for the other priority areas: Integrated 
Sustainable Rural Development and Regional Integration. These Theme Groups will serve as 
the main mechanism for implementing and monitoring the implementation of the UNDAF 
through the development of multi-year work-plans with clear goals and objectives. 26
The work-plans will spell out the resource requirements by agency and the monitoring 
and evaluation plans. As is proposed in the current HIV/AIDS Theme Group work-plan, 
monitoring and evaluation mechanisms will include quarterly and annual review with the 
Government and other relevant partners. The monthly meetings of the Heads of UN Agencies 
will serve as the steering mechanism to review and validate the cooperation between agencies 
on the three priority areas. Regular feedback from the theme group chairs will be included. 
The work-plans will reflect the ongoing activities related to the priority areas of each 
agency. They will also identify the areas for collaborative or parallel programming as well as 
opportunities for joint programming. The HIV/AIDS Theme group has identified three key 
flagships for joint programming. In this context the UN Country Team agrees to introduce 
urgent streamlining of administrative and substantive reporting procedures to facilitate 
parallel / joint programming and to enhance local implementation capacity. This will entail 
the development and deployment of joint financial and substantive progress monitoring 
information systems to enable joint programming and decentralised implementation.
The government of South Africa has identified an UNDAF focal point within the 
Presidency to support the day-to-day processes of the UNDAF. It is envisaged further that on 
an annual basis the UN Country Team meet with the Directors-General cluster on the social 
sector, which will serve as the main “home” for the UNDAF, to review progress and 
setbacks, and recommend any necessary adjustments or updates. 
V - PROGRAMME RESOURCE FRAMEWORK
Individual agency allocations will be determined at the time that the agency 
programmes are being drawn up. Although it is desirable to provide an indication of the 
resources which may be thus committed, the UNCT decided in the final analysis that such an 
exercise would be much too hypothetical in the current state of affairs and at this moment in 
the programming of UN resources, for a period which is starting in eighteen months.
